items.headline: UK adds 38 Russia sanctions designations across oil, shadow fleet, crypto, payments and military supply routes
items.what_happened: On 8 October 2026 the UK Government announced 38 new Russia sanctions designations. The announced targets include two Russian oil companies, 12 oil tankers described as part of Russia's shadow fleet, crypto exchanges and payment platforms, and suppliers of goods the UK, US and EU consider important to Russia's military production. The Government says it suspects the named crypto and payment entities are being used to circumvent financial sanctions, and says two of them processed or facilitated transactions with the A7 network. Those statements describe the Government's stated basis for the action and should not be extended to other platforms without evidence.
items.why_it_matters: The package reaches several parts of the same evasion system: oil production, vessels, payment channels, crypto infrastructure and procurement of controlled goods. A name-only screening response would miss the connection between those layers. Because the package includes companies, individuals and vessels, firms need to ingest the underlying list records and identifiers rather than rely only on the headline total.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis, not a requirement stated in the announcement. Firms should check that the 8 October list changes reached customer, counterparty, vessel and payment screening, then review ownership and control, vessel identifiers, trade routes and relevant crypto or payment relationships around any match. Historical exposure review should identify funds or economic resources that may need to remain frozen or be reported, but the date and legal effect of each designation must be preserved so earlier activity is not treated as retrospectively prohibited. Where a payment or trade alert links to the A7 network, treat the network connection as an investigation lead and verify it against transaction and counterparty evidence rather than infer it from geography alone.

items.headline: FCA survey finds 63% of corporate finance firms combine compliance with other duties while 90% use third-party support
items.what_happened: On 8 October 2026 the FCA published results from a survey of 411 corporate finance firms, to which 382 responded. Most respondents were small: 64% had nine or fewer employees and 89% had fewer than 50. The FCA says 63% reported a compliance function that was not dedicated solely to compliance, while 90% used some form of third-party compliance support. Forty-seven per cent reported carrying out all activities covered by the survey. Reported gaps included 90 firms without arrangements for whistleblowers to disclose concerns, 82 without a breach register, 82 where compliance did not attend management-body meetings, and 140 where regulatory compliance was not part of staff performance assessment. These are self-reported survey results, not findings from direct testing of every respondent.
items.why_it_matters: The FCA is not prescribing one staffing model or saying that combined roles and outsourced support are automatically inadequate. Its focus is whether compliance has enough presence, authority, access and independence to challenge the business, and whether senior management remains actively involved. The survey therefore provides a practical benchmark for governance weaknesses that can exist even where a firm completes routine compliance tasks.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis, not an FCA finding about any particular firm. Corporate finance firms should test whether compliance is involved before important decisions are fixed, whether revenue-generating duties create a conflict, whether breach and whistleblowing information reaches the management body, and whether third-party advice is independently understood and challenged. A proportionate model can be small or outsourced, but the evidence should show who owns decisions, how conflicts are managed and how senior management verifies that the arrangement works in practice.

items.headline: FinCEN withdraws proposed unhosted-wallet reporting rules and its proposed special measure for virtual-currency mixing
items.what_happened: On 5 October 2026 FinCEN announced that it was withdrawing two proposed digital-asset rules, with the Federal Register withdrawals effective on 6 October. The first was a 2020 proposal for banks and money service businesses to report, keep records and verify customers for certain transactions involving convertible virtual currency or digital assets held in unhosted or specified foreign-hosted wallets. The second withdrew both a 2023 finding that international convertible virtual currency mixing was a class of transactions of primary money laundering concern and a proposed special measure requiring enhanced records and reports. FinCEN says it will take no further action on the unhosted-wallet proposal. It also says illicit actors continue to use mixers, that it will continue monitoring mixer activity and that it may take future steps.
items.why_it_matters: The action removes two proposals and the mixing finding; it does not repeal existing Bank Secrecy Act duties or establish that unhosted wallets and mixing activity are low risk. For firms that had tracked the proposals as future change, the need to prepare for those proposed requirements falls away. Existing customer due diligence, suspicious activity monitoring and sanctions controls continue to depend on the firm's actual legal scope and risk exposure.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis, not FinCEN guidance. US banks and money service businesses should close or reclassify these two items in regulatory change registers, remove implementation work tied only to the withdrawn proposals, and retain controls that address risks already covered by current law and the firm's risk assessment. Firms outside the United States should first establish whether a US entity, customer, transaction or correspondent relationship creates a relevant nexus before treating the withdrawal as operationally applicable. Neither proposal should be used as a reason to disable blockchain analytics or suspicious activity review without a separate control assessment.

items.headline: OFSI clarifies that single-person specific licences are no longer needed after delisting and do not revive on relisting
items.what_happened: On 9 October 2026 OFSI added FAQ 205 on what happens to specific licences when a designated person is delisted. OFSI says UK financial sanctions cease to apply to that person or entity on delisting. A specific licence that concerns only the delisted person and no other relevant sanctions is no longer needed, and the holder does not need to ask OFSI to revoke it or contact OFSI about its status. Pending applications that cease to be required will be closed. If the person or entity is later relisted, earlier specific licences do not reactivate and a new licence application is required.
items.why_it_matters: The guidance separates three events that case-management systems can otherwise collapse: delisting ends the relevant restrictions for that person, an existing single-person licence becomes unnecessary, and a later relisting starts a new position rather than reviving the old licence. It also preserves an important qualification: the answer applies where the licence concerns only the delisted person and no other relevant sanctions.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis, not legal advice. Licence records should identify every person, prohibition and sanctions basis they cover, so a delisting triggers a scoped review rather than automatic closure of the whole case. Controls should stop relying on a licence that is no longer needed, record why any pending application was closed, and require a fresh legal and licensing assessment if the person is relisted. Before releasing funds or resuming activity, firms should still check for other designations, ownership or control, sectoral prohibitions and any separate restrictions affecting the transaction.
